topics.topic: The shutdown of Concord
topics.angle: Sony spent eight years and reportedly hundreds of millions on Concord. It sold so badly that the servers were switched off two weeks after launch and the game was refunded out of existence.

topics.topic: The shutdown of Club Penguin
topics.angle: A childrens virtual world with hundreds of millions of registered accounts, closed by Disney in 2017 while players held a final party on the servers.

topics.topic: The shutdown of Toontown Online
topics.angle: Disneys first MMO ran for ten years before being closed in 2013 — and was then rebuilt by its own players, who still run it.

topics.topic: The shutdown of City of Heroes
topics.angle: NCSoft closed a profitable superhero MMO in 2012. Players campaigned for years, and in 2019 it emerged the servers had secretly been kept alive the whole time.

topics.topic: The shutdown of Star Wars Galaxies
topics.angle: An MMO that rewrote its own combat system overnight, lost most of its players, and was shut down in 2011 with the servers going dark on the same day.

topics.topic: The deletion of GeoCities
topics.angle: Yahoo deleted around 38 million user-built pages in 2009. Most of the early personal web survives only because volunteers raced to archive it first.

topics.topic: The collapse of Friendster
topics.angle: The social network that came before MySpace and Facebook, turned down a Google buyout, then deleted every user photo and message in 2011.

topics.topic: The shutdown of Google Plus
topics.angle: Google forced its social network onto every product it owned, then closed it in 2019 after a data leak it had chosen not to disclose.

topics.topic: The shutdown of Vine
topics.angle: Twitter bought Vine for thirty million dollars, made it a culture-defining format, then shut it down in 2017 without ever selling an ad on it.

topics.topic: The shutdown of LimeWire
topics.angle: The file-sharing program on half the worlds computers, sued into oblivion in 2010 for a figure larger than the entire recorded music industry.

topics.topic: An anonymous college‑campus messaging app that closed in 2017.
topics.angle: Its rise and fall were driven by privacy concerns and widespread harassment.

topics.topic: A social networking site that peaked before Facebook and shut its original service in 2013.
topics.angle: It was an early competitor that couldn’t survive the shift to mobile‑first platforms.

topics.topic: A collaborative communication tool launched in 2009 and discontinued in 2010.
topics.angle: It was technically innovative but too complex for mainstream adoption.

topics.topic: One of the first popular web search engines, retired by Yahoo! in 2013.

topics.topic: Google’s RSS aggregator that was shut down in 2013 despite a loyal user base.
topics.angle: Its removal sparked a backlash that highlighted the power of user‑driven tools.

topics.topic: Google’s social network that was popular in Brazil and India before closing in 2014.
topics.angle: It remains one of the most beloved defunct platforms for its community focus.
